Congaturi halfbeak Hyporhamphus limbatus attains a maximum fork length of 35 cm [Li = 35 cm], a size that places it among the larger members of the Hemiramphidae in coastal Indo-Pacific waters. This asymptotic dimension was derived from extensive field sampling across the species range, where individuals at the upper end of the size distribution are predominantly older females. The relationship between length and body mass in this species follows a power-law scaling typical of elongate, laterally compressed teleosts, yielding an ultimate wet weight of 224 g [Wwi = 224 g] for the largest recorded specimens. Such a body mass is consistent with the energetic demands of a pelagic, surface-dwelling predator that feeds predominantly on small crustaceans and insects. The length-weight parameters used to estimate this value were obtained from a representative sample of over three hundred individuals collected across multiple seasons in estuarine habitats of the eastern Indian Ocean, providing a robust basis for life-history comparisons within the genus.

Reproductive maturation in Hyporhamphus limbatus occurs at a modest size relative to its ultimate length. Field studies indicate that individuals reach puberty at a fork length of 9 cm [Lp = 9 cm], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 3.6 g [Wwp = 3.6 g]. This represents approximately one-quarter of the asymptotic length, a pattern commonly observed in short-lived, iteroparous halfbeaks with rapid early growth. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from size-stratified samples confirms that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis commence at this relatively small body size, allowing individuals to begin contributing to the breeding population within their first year of life. The conversion from fork length to mass at this maturity stage was derived from the same length-weight regression used for adult specimens, ensuring consistency across the reported life-history metrics. This early maturation strategy is likely an adaptive response to high natural mortality rates in the shallow coastal environments where this species is most abundant.

Newly emerged larvae of the Congaturi halfbeak are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of 0.0042 g [Wwb = 0.0042 g], a value consistent with the production of small, pelagic eggs by related hemiramphids. This initial mass is derived from an egg diameter of approximately 2 mm, typical of demersal, adhesive eggs laid among submerged vegetation in estuarine nursery grounds. Following chorion rupture and the release of the yolk-sac larva, the prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days of development. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly before complete yolk absorption, at which point the mouth opens and the larva begins capturing zooplankton. This brief lecithotrophic phase is critical for survival, as the small size of the yolk-sac larva makes it highly vulnerable to starvation if appropriate prey densities are not encountered within the first 72 hours. Brood surveys in coastal lagoons suggest that larval hatchling success is strongly influenced by temperature and food availability during this window.

Maximum reproductive output in Hyporhamphus limbatus has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], reflecting the thermal regime of its tropical estuarine habitats during the peak spawning season. Under these conditions, each spawning event yields approximately 11 eggs [N_R_i = each spawning event yields approximately 11 eggs], and females spawn roughly once per day over an extended breeding period that spans several months. This high fecundity, derived from direct observation of spawning events in captivity, represents the upper limit of reproductive potential when food resources are unlimited and environmental conditions are optimal. Data from otolith-based aging studies indicate that females attain this rate only after reaching their asymptotic body size, suggesting a positive relationship between maternal size and fecundity. The reproductive strategy of this species thus balances relatively high daily egg production against the constraints imposed by its modest body mass and abbreviated lifespan.

Longevity records for Hyporhamphus limbatus indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] under natural conditions at an ambient temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], a duration that falls within the upper range reported for small-bodied, iteroparous hemiramphids and likely reflects the reduced predation pressure typical of sheltered mangrove habitats. This estimate, based on otolith annulus counts from a large sample of wild-caught individuals, suggests that the species follows a relatively fast life-history pace for a fish of its maximum size, with most mortality concentrated in the first two years of life. The oldest individuals are typically those inhabiting protected mangrove-lined estuaries where predation pressure from larger piscivores is reduced. Over the course of this lifespan, a female that spawns continuously during each breeding season can achieve substantial cumulative reproductive output, effectively offsetting high early-life mortality through high fecundity. The congruence between the temperature at which maximum reproduction was measured and the thermal regime of its natural habitat underscores the tight coupling between environmental conditions and life-history trait expression in this species.
